name: Brownish Olive
lede: Brownish Olive is a dull, dark olive that leans to brown, among the most common muted colors in old paintings.

sections.title: The name
sections.body:
The name is descriptive, from Ridgway's 1912 atlas and the later ISCC-NBS system, block 94, and it sits near [[umber]] [1]. Nothing in the books points to a single pigment behind it.

Paterson does note that litharge, a by-product of melting white lead also called massicot, was described as a yellow or brownish olive color [3]. That is a dictionary gloss on one material, and it does not make the swatch a litharge color [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Brownish Olive appears in 22.43% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, as photographed [2]. It is more common than 99% of the named colors, and it peaks in the 1100s at 24.0% of that century's paintings [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 32% of cases [2]. Its most devoted painter is Jean-Charles Cazin, in 8 of 16 works here [2]. Aged varnish pushes many greens and yellows toward this swatch, so treat it as how paintings photograph [2].

origin.named_after: descriptive; origin of the name undocumented
